spec.title: PodBay platform backends and portable pod contract

status.comment: Cross-platform requirement approved by the owner. Linux has partial runtime evidence; macOS and Windows have no native acceptance receipt yet.

p.scope: PodBay is a cross-platform agent runtime for Linux, macOS, and Windows. A successful Linux implementation alone is not cross-platform completion. Each supported platform must pass its own process-survival, tree-stop, terminal, durable-replay, and authority gates before that platform is advertised as operational. An unavailable backend returns a typed unsupported capability before any side effect.

p.portable-contract: The public Rust and podbay/1 contracts address SessionId, RunId, AttemptId, PodId, ResourceId, incarnation, command identity, receipt stage, cursor, scope, and capability. They do not require a systemd unit, cgroup path, Unix socket, launchd label, Windows handle, or native PID. Those values are platform-specific attestation evidence with explicit provenance.

p.backend-boundary: SupervisorBackend/1 owns launch, exact-manifest reconciliation, process-tree identity, manager-independent pod lifetime, reattachment, bounded stop, and descendant reaping. TerminalBackend/1 owns PTY or pseudoconsole creation, output, input, resize, and process attachment. LocalControlTransport/1 owns authenticated local requests. DurableFiles/1 owns private creation, append durability, atomic replacement, directory or equivalent metadata durability, and corruption reporting. No backend may infer provider consumption from process or terminal transport success.

p.linux: The Linux backend may use user systemd units, cgroup evidence, /proc process start identity, POSIX PTYs, and Unix-domain sockets. A pod unit is independent of the manager unit. The current Linux slices remain partial until durable spool, authority, and cold rebind gates pass.

p.macos: The macOS backend uses a user launchd agent or an equivalently supervised user service for manager-independent pods, platform process start identity and process-group containment, POSIX PTYs, and authenticated Unix-domain control. A user agent's logout lifecycle is explicit; survival across logout is not claimed without a separately validated daemon or service configuration.

p.windows: The Windows backend uses an independently living pod process or service, a pod-owned Job Object for child-tree cleanup, creation-time process identity, an access-controlled named pipe for local control, and ConPTY for interactive console resources. A kill-on-close Job handle must not be held only by the restartable manager. Parent-job breakaway restrictions and unsupported hosts are reported rather than bypassed silently.

p.identity: An OS account or Unix UID alone is not an agent principal: sibling pods may share one account. The authenticated transport binds a request to registered pod/process incarnation or a scoped issued capability, with platform process evidence and credential generation. Human owner access is a separate grant. Backend replacement advances the relevant fence and never adopts an unverified process by PID alone.

p.durability: SQLite command and event semantics are shared across platforms. Manifest, spool, and checkpoint writes must use the platform's proven durable-file operations; POSIX rename/fsync assumptions cannot be copied into Windows code without an equivalent replacement and flush protocol. Reopening truncated or corrupt state reports an exact gap or unknown state and never retries uncertain input automatically.

p.conformance: Each platform has focused native fixtures for manager restart while coordinator and worker pods continue; exact pod/process identity on reattach; no duplicate launch after ambiguous admission; descendant cleanup on pod stop; two read-only terminal viewers; exclusive fenced input and resize; durable cursor replay or explicit gap; same-account sibling scope refusal; and crash windows around input and filesystem sync. Cross-target compilation is a useful preliminary check but does not replace native runtime receipts.
